prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Iran has condemned the kidnapping of one of its diplomats in northwest Pakistan on Thursday, calling it an "act of terrorism," an Iranian foreign ministry spokesman said. Pakistani policemen inspect a bullet-riddled car of a kidnapped Iranian diplomat on Thursday. "Pakistan should do its best to protect foreign diplomats and their residential places," the spokesman Hassan Qashqavi said, according to Iran's state-run IRNA news agency. At least four gunmen abducted Heshmatollah Attarzadeh near his home in Peshawar as he headed to work at the Iranian consulate, according to Pakistani police and Iranian diplomatic officials. His bodyguard, a Pakistani police officer, was shot and killed when the two men tried to resist, a Peshawar police official said. Pakistan's Foreign Minister Shah Mahmood Qureshi also "strongly condemned" the attack, and informed Iran that the government "will take all necessary measures for his safe and early recovery." Attarzadeh is a commercial attache for the Iranian consulate in Peshawar. It is the second attack targeting a foreign worker in Peshawar in two days. An American aid worker was shot and killed outside the Iranian consulate in Peshawar on Wednesday. Stephen Vance worked for a non-profit foundation funded by the U.S. Agency for International Development that helped find jobs for people in Pakistan's tribal regions, according to a statement from his employer, the Cooperative Housing Foundation International. "Stephen had fully immersed himself in the community in which he worked," the statement said. "He dressed traditionally and even sent his children to local schools." Vance, 52, a native of California, is survived by his wife and five children -- all of whom lived with him in Peshawar -- CHF International official Bill Holbrook told CNN. The attacks come less than three months after gunmen opened fire on a vehicle carrying the senior U.S. diplomat in Peshawar, Lynne Tracy. She escaped unharmed. Peshawar is the capital of Pakistan's North West Frontier Province, an area rife with Islamic extremists and the site of recent clashes between security forces and militants. In late June, Pakistan's military launched an offensive in the province -- the biggest push against extremists in the tribal region since the civilian government took power in March. Islamic militants vowed to retaliate. Since then, militants have launched several deadly attacks. Pakistan's new government has tried to negotiate a deal with militants as part of its efforts to bypass military might and achieve peace through talks.

**Iran condemns kidnapping of diplomat in Pakistan**

**PESHAWAR, Pakistan** — Iran strongly condemned the kidnapping of one of its diplomats in northwestern Pakistan on Thursday after gunmen ambushed his vehicle in the city of Peshawar, killing his bodyguard and seizing the envoy, Pakistani and Iranian officials said.

Heshmatollah Attarzadeh, an Iranian commercial attaché, was abducted as he traveled from his home to the Iranian consulate in Peshawar, a city close to Pakistan’s tribal areas along the Afghan border. Authorities said several armed men intercepted his car, opened fire and forced him into another vehicle before fleeing.

A Pakistani security guard assigned to protect the diplomat was killed in the attack, officials said. Police launched a search operation in the area, but no group immediately claimed responsibility.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry denounced the kidnapping as a “terrorist act” and called on Pakistan to take urgent steps to secure Attarzadeh’s release and protect Iranian diplomatic personnel. Tehran also expressed condolences over the killing of the bodyguard.

Peshawar has seen a rise in violence as Taliban-linked militants and criminal groups have expanded attacks and kidnappings in the region. The abduction of Attarzadeh follows a series of recent attacks targeting foreigners and foreign-linked workers in Pakistan.

Earlier, an American aid worker was shot dead in Peshawar, and foreign engineers and diplomats have been targeted in separate incidents in the country’s northwest and southwest. Militants and criminal gangs have increasingly used kidnappings to seek ransom, prisoner exchanges or political leverage.

Pakistani officials said security had been tightened around foreign missions and residences in Peshawar after the attack. The city, long considered a gateway to Afghanistan, has become increasingly dangerous amid the spillover of militancy from Pakistan’s tribal belt.

The kidnapping is likely to increase pressure on Pakistan’s government to improve security for diplomats and foreign workers operating in volatile parts of the country.

counterfactuals.output:
**Foreign Officials and Aid Workers Targeted in Peshawar Amid Rising Militant Violence**

**PESHAWAR, Pakistan —** A series of brazen attacks on foreign officials and aid workers in Peshawar has underscored the deteriorating security situation in northwestern Pakistan, a region increasingly affected by militant networks operating along the Afghan border.

The violence has included the kidnapping of an Iranian diplomat, the killing of an American aid worker, and earlier attacks on U.S. diplomatic personnel, raising alarm among foreign missions and humanitarian organizations working in the area.

The most dramatic incident occurred when **Heshmatollah Attarzadeh**, an Iranian diplomat serving at the Iranian consulate in Peshawar, was abducted by gunmen while traveling through the city. Attackers reportedly ambushed his vehicle, killing his police guard before seizing him. The kidnapping highlighted the vulnerability of diplomatic staff in Peshawar, long considered a key hub for international engagement with Pakistan’s tribal areas and neighboring Afghanistan.

Iran condemned the abduction and pressed Pakistani authorities to secure Attarzadeh’s release. The attack also placed additional strain on security services already struggling to contain militant activity in the region. Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, sits near the former federally administered tribal areas, where Pakistani Taliban factions, criminal gangs, and other armed groups have operated.

The kidnapping came amid shock over the killing of **Stephen Vance**, an American aid worker associated with U.S.-funded development efforts in Pakistan. Vance was shot dead in Peshawar when gunmen opened fire on his vehicle. His killing sent a chilling message to foreign assistance organizations, many of which had been working on education, governance, health, and reconstruction projects in Pakistan’s northwest.

U.S. officials condemned the attack, describing Vance as a civilian working to support development and improve conditions for ordinary Pakistanis. His death raised questions about whether foreign aid projects could continue safely in the area, especially as militants increasingly viewed Western-backed development programs as extensions of foreign policy.

The attacks followed earlier assaults on U.S. diplomatic targets in Peshawar. In one incident, gunmen fired on a vehicle carrying American diplomatic personnel, though the occupants escaped without serious injury. Such attacks reflected a widening threat environment in which foreign diplomats, consulate staff, aid workers, and local employees of international organizations were all at heightened risk.

Pakistani authorities increased security around consulates, international offices, and residential areas frequented by foreigners, including Peshawar’s University Town district, where many aid agencies and diplomatic staff maintained offices or residences. However, the city’s dense urban layout and proximity to militant strongholds made it difficult to prevent targeted attacks.

Security analysts said the incidents appeared to demonstrate a shift in tactics by militant and extremist groups, from attacks on Pakistani security forces and government installations to targeted operations against foreign nationals and international organizations. Kidnappings, assassinations, and ambushes offered militants both propaganda value and leverage over governments.

“These attacks were intended to show that militants could strike high-profile targets even in heavily policed urban areas,” one regional security analyst said. “They also created fear among foreign missions and aid agencies, which was one of the attackers’ main objectives.”

The growing insecurity placed Pakistan’s government under pressure from foreign governments to improve protection for diplomats and international workers. At the same time, local officials warned that militants were exploiting porous borders, weak law enforcement capacity, and instability in nearby tribal districts.

For aid organizations, the killings and kidnappings forced difficult choices. Some restricted staff movement, hired additional security, or relocated personnel. Others suspended field operations altogether, limiting humanitarian and development work in communities already affected by conflict and poverty.

The attacks in Peshawar became part of a broader pattern of violence gripping Pakistan’s northwest during that period. Militants opposed to the Pakistani state, the United States, and allied governments increasingly targeted symbols of foreign presence, including embassies, consulates, aid agencies, supply routes, and local partners.

The kidnapping of Heshmatollah Attarzadeh, the killing of Stephen Vance, and the earlier attacks on U.S. diplomats collectively marked a grim escalation in threats facing foreign officials and aid workers in Peshawar. They also illustrated the city’s transformation from a diplomatic and humanitarian gateway into one of the most dangerous operating environments in the region.

**Iran demands action after diplomat abducted in Pakistan**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan —** Iran has urged Pakistan to take urgent action after an Iranian diplomat was abducted in the northwestern city of Peshawar, an incident that underscores the worsening security situation along Pakistan’s frontier with Afghanistan.

The diplomat, identified in Iranian and Pakistani media reports as a senior official at Iran’s consulate in Peshawar, was seized by gunmen while traveling in the city. His Pakistani driver was reportedly killed in the attack.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry condemned the abduction and called on Pakistani authorities to ensure the diplomat’s safe release. Tehran also pressed Islamabad to strengthen protection for Iranian diplomatic staff and facilities in Pakistan.

Pakistani officials said security forces had launched a search operation and were investigating who was behind the kidnapping. No group immediately claimed responsibility.

Peshawar, the capital of the former North West Frontier Province — now known as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — has been a frequent target of militant attacks and kidnappings. The province borders Pakistan’s tribal areas and lies close to Afghanistan, making it a key corridor for militant groups, criminal networks and smuggling routes.

In recent years, militants linked to the Pakistani Taliban and other extremist factions have expanded their influence in parts of the northwest, including areas near Peshawar, Swat and the tribal belt. The region has seen bombings, attacks on security forces, assassinations of local officials and abductions of foreigners and diplomats.

Pakistan’s government has carried out military operations in several parts of the northwest, but militants have continued to exploit rugged terrain, weak governance and cross-border movement. The violence has raised concerns among neighboring countries, including Iran, which shares a long border with Pakistan and has previously accused militants of using Pakistani territory to stage attacks.

The abduction of the Iranian diplomat adds to pressure on Pakistan’s government to restore order in the region and protect foreign missions operating in high-risk areas.
